Article Title: 'Vanished from tracking system': How Panama-flagged cargo ship with 24 on board sank off Odisha coast
Article Text:
Panama-flagged MV Ocean Winner sinks in Bay of Bengal; 22 crew members remain missing

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A Panama-flagged bulk carrier carrying 24 crew members sank in the Bay of Bengal off Odisha after reportedly disappearing from maritime tracking systems, triggering a large-scale search and rescue operation by authorities.The vessel, MV Ocean Winner, was carrying an iron ore cargo and had departed from Paradip Port. It was reportedly headed for Singapore, with an estimated arrival date of August 27. The 225-metre-long ship was last reported more than 200 nautical miles off the Odisha coast before communication with it was lost, news agency ANI reported.The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) received information late Saturday about the loss of contact with the vessel and a request for search and rescue assistance from Victory Star Group Co Ltd.The ship had 24 crew members on board, including 20 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi national.Following the distress alert, MRCC (SVP) activated the International Safety Net and diverted merchant vessel MT AISOPOS to the area to search for MV Ocean Winner and any liferafts.The merchant vessel subsequently rescued two survivors from separate liferafts at around 8pm.The Indian Coast Guard also mobilised ICGS Varad and ICGS Anmol for the rescue operation, while ICGS Vijit was deployed from Sri Vijaya Puram to reinforce the search.Officials said efforts were continuing to locate the remaining crew members. The circumstances that led to the vessel losing communication and sinking were not immediately clear.According to MarineTraffic, MV Ocean Winner was a Panama-flagged bulk carrier measuring 225 metres in length and 32.26 metres in width.
Article Summary: Panama-flagged mv ocean winner sinks in bay of bengal; 22 crew members remain missing. The ship had 24 crew members on board, including 20 chinese nationals, three myanmar nationals and one bangladeshi national. The circumstances that led to the vessel losing communication and sinking were not immediately clear.

Article Title: Jaishankar to visit Moscow on August 23-24
Article Text:
Jaishankar to visit Moscow to co-chair India-Russia trade, economic cooperation meet and hold talks with Lavrov

NEW DELHI: At the invitation of Russia's first deputy PM Denis Manturov, external affairs minister S Jaishankar will visit Moscow on Aug 23-24 to co-chair the 27th Session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC).Under the IRIGC-TEC mechanism, sectoral working groups focus on priority areas such as Trade & Economic Cooperation, Industrial Cooperation, Energy Cooperation, Chemicals and Fertilisers, Information and Communication Technology, Pharmaceuticals and Mining. During the visit, Jaishankar will also meet his counterpart Sergey Lavrov and discuss regional and global issues. The American tariff threat-particularly the recent legislative push in Washington-is likely to figure in the meetings.The visit will also prepare the groundwork for upcoming high-level engagements between the two countries.
Article Summary: Jaishankar to visit moscow to co-chair india-russia trade, economic cooperation meet and hold talks with lavrov. The american tariff threat-particularly the recent legislative push in washington-is likely to figure in the meetings. The visit will also prepare the groundwork for upcoming high-level engagements between the two countries.

The Federation of Seafarers and Indian Seafarers Union (FSUI) has released an old video showing a vessel carrying 22 crew members, including 21 Indians, coming under attack in the Strait of Hormuz on April 22.The footage shows several small boats surrounding the vessel, an RPG being fired and seafarers rushing to the ship’s alleyways to take cover as the confrontation unfolded.The union also released images showing crew members taking cover while the vessel was under attack.“These were not pirates. They were naval forces of the IRGC,” the FSUI said in a post on X.The union added that the footage highlighted the risks faced by seafarers in the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that advisories and guidelines alone could not ensure their safety.“Innocent seafarers need the assured presence of naval forces to truly protect them,” the FSUI said.The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) recently said 166 Indian seafarers remained in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz region, including 125 aboard six Indian-flagged vessels and 41 working on foreign-flagged ships.In an update on August 4, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways said 3,972 Indian seafarers had been repatriated from the Gulf region, highlighting the scale of the effort to bring them out of the conflict zone.India is the world’s second-largest supplier of seafarers after the Philippines, with 311,936 personnel accounting for 12.16 per cent of the global maritime workforce, according to the BIMCO-ICS Seafarer Workforce Report 2026. Indian officers account for 13.41 per cent of the global officer workforce, while 171,218 Indian ratings make up 11.29 per cent of the global ratings workforce.The large presence of Indian seafarers in the region has also resulted in casualties since the Iran war began. Last month, the MEA said Indian seafarers had recorded the highest number of fatalities among all nationalities in attacks on commercial shipping.The government later informed Parliament that 10 Indian seafarers were among the 16 Indian nationals killed in the Middle East conflict.

Article Title: 'We fought wars with Pakistan too, but China will be India's main competitor': Ex-Army chief
Article Text:
General MM Naravane (Retd) on China and Pakistan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former Army chief General MM Naravane (Retired) on Thursday described China as India's "main competitor" in the years ahead, despite India having fought wars with both China and Pakistan."Pakistan and China are a totally different ballgame. We have fought wars with both of them. We have unsettled borders. So they will always remain on our radar as a threat, as a challenge," PTI quoted Naravane as saying at a book launch event in New Delhi.However, he distinguished between the two, saying India's immediate focus on Pakistan was driven largely by the continuing threat of terrorism, while describing China as a "competitor" rather than an "enemy." He emphasised that he had "purposely" used the term "competitor" for China."We have fought major wars with Pakistan, and because of their continued support to terrorism, our attention is towards our western borders. But I think we are very clear that in the long term and in the years to come, China is going to be our main competitor. And I purposely use the word competitor and not enemy," Naravane said.Naravane, who was Chief of Army Staff during the 2020 Ladakh clashes with China and led India's response, further stated that the two countries would be competitors across multiple domains, including politics, economics, trade and military affairs."They are going to be our main competitor in all fields. Political, economic, trade, and of course military also. And wherever there is competition, there is always a little bit of conflict," the retired Army general observed.He emphasised that India should seek to manage such differences through dialogue and diplomatic mechanisms rather than resorting to force."It is up to us to try to resolve those conflicts, those differences, through the mechanisms of talks, dialogues. And taking recourse to the use of force should always be the last priority," he said.However, he also stressed that India must maintain credible military preparedness to deter any potential misadventure."There comes a moment when you realise that this is not going to happen. And therefore, you have to have a strong deterrence. That is why the armed forces have to be ready at all times. You have to have a strong deterrence to stop anybody from taking recourse to the use of force or any misadventure," he remarked.
Article Summary: General mm naravane (retd) on china and pakistan: "pakistan and china are a totally different ballgame" he emphasised that he had "purposely" used the term "competitor" for china.naravane was chief of army staff during the 2020 ladakh clashes with china.

Article Title: No more boarding pass stamps: New immigration rule for international flyers from Sept 1
Article Text:
International travelers will soon need e-boarding passes on smartphones for immigration clearance. Physical boarding passes will no longer be stamped by immigration authorities from September one. This change aims to streamline the process and reduce passenger inconvenience. A pilot project is also underway to eliminate immigration stamping for Indian passport holders. The Bureau of Immigration is implementing these modernization efforts across airports.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Passengers travelling abroad will reportedly need an e-boarding pass on their smartphones for immigration clearance from September one, as immigration authorities plan to replace the physical boarding pass, officials said.The decision was taken after the Bureau of Immigration (BOI) under the ministry of home affairs (MHA) found that the physical stamping of boarding passes, required for immigration, was inconvenient for passengers."The matter has been examined by the BOI and it has now been decided to do away with the mandatory requirement of physical boarding passes and the stamping of boarding passes at immigration counters at all international airports in the country", according to officials who spoke to PTI.“Improper or incorrect” stamping also led to errors in reading boarding passes, prompting the decision to do away with this procedure, they added.However, while physical boarding passes will continue to be accepted, they will not be stamped by the immigration authorities from September 1.Security officials said international travellers were also no longer having their boarding passes stamped by the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) during individual frisking. The passes were instead required to be produced only for clearance by immigration authorities.Notably, CISF had stopped stamping boarding passes for both domestic and international passengers several years ago.According to the officials, a pilot project is also underway to eliminate the stamping of immigration entry and exit for Indian passport holders. The process is expected to be implemented across Indian airports soon after the pilot exercise is complete.
Article Summary: International travelers will soon need e-boarding passes on smartphones for immigration clearance. Physical boarding passes will no longer be stamped by immigration authorities from september one. This change aims to streamline the process and reduce passenger inconvenience.

Article Title: One is not born, but becomes: India's drag story, from myth to modern stage
Article Text:
India has a rich but complex history of men performing femininity—one that modern drag queens are reclaiming with agency, drawing from both Indian tradition and global queer culture

The history of 'drag' in India

Contemporary drag

Drag queen: Lush Monsoon

Drag queen: Noor Sins

The most heavily quoted feminist scholar, Simone de Beauvoir, launched entire fields of feminist theory by writing - one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.To be a woman, to be feminine was never purely biological, it was also societal. You are shaped into a woman, piece by piece, experience by experience.In her rejection of the arbitrariness one would often attach to what femininity means, she made space for who some would argue is very much a queer icon and a scholar.Almost half a century later, RuPaul said: we’re all born naked, and the rest is drag.It's a strange thing, watching a philosopher and a reality show host arrive at the same conclusion from opposite directions, that gender was never the given, natural thing it pretends to be, just the costume everyone's already wearing. De Beauvoir got there through existentialism. RuPaul got there through sequins. Both arrived to the conclusion that the performance was the point all along.A common practice to define drag would be to trace its historic roots in the Indian subcontinent. Women were kept out of public spaces, be it India or the West. So when women roles had to be filled in theatrical production men would dress us as them and take up that role in the public eye.India has its own unique lineage to give to this art form, be it through mythology or folk dance and other cultural performances. In the Natyashastra, men played goddesses, heroines, demonesses, styled into femininity through gesture, costume, and the trained emotionDance forms like Kathakali, Jatra and Yakshagana still carry that inheritance. These traditions though have never termed themselves as drag and only trace lineage through reductive definitions of drag being men becoming women convincingly enough to make an audience believe it.India's mythology also builds gender transformation directly into the stories being told. In the Mahabharata's Virata Parva, Arjuna spends a year of exile disguised as Brihannala, a court dancer and music teacher, cursed by the nymph Urvashi to live without his manhood after refusing her. Shikhandi was also born a woman, raised as a warrior, and eventually granted manhood by a Yaksha to fulfil a vow of vengeance against Bhishma.None of this stayed confined to myth and stage. In Ahmedabad, on the eighth night of Navratri, men of the Barot community drape themselves in saris and jewellery to dance garba. In Kottankulangara, Kerala, thousands of men dress as women each year for Chamayavilakku, offering prayers to the goddess Durga at a temple local legend says was born from a bleeding stone, with no women present at the founding moment, boys dressed as women to complete the ritual.Outside temple and epic, there is the tradition of Launda Naach, male dancers performing in women's dress at weddings, in the North Indian belt. It's argued to be India's oldest living form of vernacular drag but it shows no interest in being called "drag".India’s modern drag is a celebration of the feminine inside a being, a lot of what we try to say it draws its lineage from was never a celebration. In some instances it was perversion and in most it was erasure of women from public spaces.A man performing femininity is not automatically a drag queen.The historical circumstances matter. Who was performing? Why were they performing? Who was watching? Who was excluded from the performance? And, crucially, who controlled what that performance meant?For Lush Monsoon, who was among the early generation of contemporary drag performers in Delhi, the relationship between these histories and modern drag is complicated by the question of agency.To her the art forms are exploitative, even if they are often posed as a celebration of queer history. She points to the gaze surrounding these traditions, and to the people who historically inhabit this gaze.“I always see them as an extension of that you are afraid of the feminine, so you are more okay with the masculine projecting as a feminine, and you putting their desire on that.”The issue, she says, is not only about the audience.A lot of the participants are queer. They are queer people from marginalised sections of society or spaces where the language of queer is not defined yet somehow exploited.A younger drag queen too, who has been in this space for around one year, held the same belief. They said that India has a culture of gender intermixing, something we can draw out as a rich queer heritage but modern drag is not a direct extension of this.“The reason that I got attracted to this form of drag, because I saw a certain amount of agency in it.”The point is not to deny India’s rich queer history but to make space for its even more vibrant present.As of today, there are only a handful of venues and spaces for drag performers. Most of the queens interviewed said Indian drag still doesn't carry the same stature as its Western counterpart, which makes it hard to find venues, build audiences, and turn performance into a sustainable career.Venues like KittySu and the Lalit chain of hotels pioneered the space, and it's now getting a push from queer collectives like the GaySi family and smaller creators trying to build safer rooms for queens and their audiences.Yet, reaching a wider audience in the digital era will take a digital push. Every queen interviewed named the same first encounter with drag as an art form: RuPaul's Drag Race. The show cemented its place in queer history, but there's a need for an Indian platform that celebrates queerness and the art form on its own terms, instead of reducing it to comedy.Older drag queens have long faced the accusation of importing a Western culture that maligns Indian heritage. But that heritage has always had space for queer stories. It was colonialism that maligned it, criminalising hijra communities and policing gender through an imported Victorian morality, codified in 1861 as Section 377, a law that stayed on the books for 157 years until the Supreme Court struck it down in 2018.Getting there took decades of work the current generation didn't have to do from scratch. Earlier drag queens fought not just for legal recognition but for the art form itself – pulling it apart from the crass, punchline version of drag Indian television has long been comfortable with.Noor Sins, a younger queen, put it simply: that fight mattered because it meant queens her age could grow up with contemporary, Indian, queer icons to look up to, not borrowed ones.It is perhaps here that the history of Indian drag and what Indian drag is becomes more interesting. In some sense drag always existed but for a lot of contemporary queens what did not exist was the ability to see themselves in the person performing it.The queens performing on stage are taking a form that has so often been used to make femininity into spectacle and making spectacle something they control. They are borrowing from the West without necessarily belonging to it, and drawing from Indian history without pretending that every man who ever wore a sari was a drag queen.The world is changing, the queens coming up now get to inherit something their predecessors had to build: a language, a community, spaces to perform, and most importantly, people who look like them already standing on a stage. But the stage has to become bigger, and the language more universal.De Beauvoir never wrote about drag. But she wrote the sentence that explains why it matters: one is not born, but becomes. For the queens performing in India today, that becoming is not simply about becoming a woman through makeup and dresses. It is about becoming visible to themselves, and then to one another, in a form that did not always give them someone to see.
Article Summary: India has a rich but complex history of men performing femininity. Modern drag queens are reclaiming with agency, drawing from both indian tradition and global queer culture. In the natyashastra, men played goddesses, heroines, demonesses, styled into femininity through gesture and costume.

Article Title: India can help US find a way from Iran trap: Former British PM Boris Johnson
Article Text:
Boris Johnson calls US war on Iran a 'mistake', urges India, US and UK to help reopen Hormuz and pressure Russia over Ukraine

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former British PM Boris Johnson Saturday urged India, US and Britain to coordinate with one another on ending the Iran conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while calling Washington's war a "mistake" and pressing New Delhi to pressure Russia to end the Ukraine war. He also said that Putin is fated to lose the war with Ukraine.Speaking at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum, Johnson said it was "totally deranged" to believe that regime change in Iran could be achieved through air strikes. Iran must be prevented from acquiring nuclear weapons and sponsoring terrorism, but change in the country had to come from within. "We've got to find a deal with Iran," he said, adding the countries should work together to lower oil prices and get ships moving.Johnson faulted US for not consulting Britain before the war, saying it had walked into an "obvious trap". Yet, he described America as a hegemon he would prefer over China and said that allies must help it "back out" of the cul-de-sac. Trump, he added, was consultative and liked advice from friends, including Modi.Turning to Ukraine, Johnson told his Indian audience not to believe "propaganda" that Putin was in a position to win; he was "fated to lose" against Ukrainians' desire for freedom.He backed giving Ukraine Tomahawks, transferring $140 billion of Putin's cash held in Brussels and stopping trade in sanctioned Russian oil. Only Putin, not Trump or Zelenskyy, could end the war, he said.Acknowledging India's "particular position" and historical closeness to Russia, Johnson said the conflict would not end without greater pressure on Moscow. He also called for deeper India-UK and India-US military cooperation, saying it would be "much more sensible".Johnson was effusive about India and Modi. "The Indian story today is a really wonderful story," he said, predicting an "incredible future" for India because it is a democracy and a free country. He also hailed the India-UK FTA, negotiations for which began when he was PM.
Article Summary: Boris johnson calls us war on iran a'mistake', urges india, us and uk to help reopen hormuz and pressure russia over ukraine. He also said that putin is fated to lose the war with ukraine. Johnson said it was "totally deranged" to believe that regime change could be achieved through air strikes.

Article Title: India-US ties to define global stage, trade deal coming: Sergio Gor
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The India-US relationship is anchored in trust and friendship between PM Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump, said US ambassador to India Sergio Gor. The ambassador also said that the bilateral trade agreement under discussion is "on its way" while pointing to surging trade numbers."The numbers don't lie. If you look at the trajectory of our relationship, just go by the numbers. And so, 15 years ago, our bilateral trade was $20 billion. Today, it's $240 billion. And it's continuing to grow. A lot of it is the legal technical language that needs to be sorted out. So, I'm optimistic we'll get done," he said.Gor said that the two countries have a natural partnership and one which will define the global stage."We have two of the biggest giants in business. We have two of the biggest economies.Us ,working together, is a natural partnership. And you can look decade by decade and forget the daily bumps... the relationship has been doing this decade by decade and growing," said the ambassador.Backing the Quad mechanism, Gor said US secretary of state Marco Rubio will be visiting India again this year. Article Title: 'Ties must serve mutual interest': EAM Jaishankar on Bangladesh
Article Text:
Jaishankar said India’s ties with Bangladesh must be based on mutual interest, while stressing that stability with China and the fight against terrorism remain key to New Delhi’s foreign policy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For any relationship to work, it has to meet the test of mutual interest, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said Saturday on the current state of ties between India and Bangladesh, particularly in the context of uncertainty over PM Tarique Rahman's visit. "It has to work for them, it has to work for us. I'm not expecting neighbours to only do what is in my interest...when you get that common landing ground, relationships work smoothly," Jaishankar said.The external affairs ministry had earlier announced that India has invited Rahman for a bilateral visit.At ET World Leaders Forum, Jaishankar reaffirmed India's position on Pakistan that dialogue and terrorism cannot coexist, and said the govt cannot be impervious to public opinion in the country.Ahead of Modi’s meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the margins of SCO and Brics summits next month, Jaishankar said both Delhi and Beijing have an interest in maintaining stability in the relationship and India needs to do business with the entire world, including China. While an official announcement is awaited, Xi will be travelling to India for Brics summit on Sept 12-13 for his first visit to the country since 2019.“But for us, the interaction... the purpose of it is finally to modernise our economy and to develop our capabilities, but even as we do so, obviously there will be trade, there will be other economic interactions with them,” said Jaishankar. He also said India remains in touch with China about business visa delays faced by Indian nationals.Recalling the 2020-24 difficult phase in the relationship, he iterated India’s position that the state of the border will determine the relationship. “Having said that, I think naturally, if assuming things are stable and the needle is more cooperative, obviously, I mean we are both very big economies in many ways, we are markets to each other.”
Article Summary: Jaishankar said india’s ties with bangladesh must be based on mutual interest, while stressing that stability with china and the fight against terrorism remain key to new delhi's foreign policy. The external affairs ministry had earlier announced that india has invited rahman for a bilateral visit.

Article Title: Ex-IAF vice-chief Kapoor says India’s 4.5-gen Tejas may not have relevance in 2030s, country must partner with global consortiums like FCAS or GCAP for 6th-gen programme
Article Text:
Air Marshal Kapoor (Retd) did not totally rule out the role of Tejas Mk2 in future

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Less than two months after retirement as the IAF's vice chief, Air Marshal Nagesh Kapoor (Retd) has slammed the delay in the delivery of Tejas (LCA) fighter jet by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited to the air force, saying, “why must it be that a machine that was promised to us so many years back with a certain set of capabilities continues to be denied to us on one pretext or the other”.In an interview to NDTV, the IAF veteran said, “Why must we be hamstrung because someone somewhere has not been able to keep their promises?”The delivery of the indigenous LCA Tejas Mk1A jets by HAL to the IAF has faced multi-year delays, primarily caused by late supplies of F404-IN20 engines by American GE company, complex mission software validation, and stringent operational requirements set by the IAF.When asked if advanced Tejas Mk-2 may be operationally relevant when it starts entering service in big numbers in mid 2030s at a time when China is already raising its fleet of its 5th-generation fighter jet, the former vice-chief said, “No, operationally, definitely no.”With China on its way to deploying 500 5th-generation J-20 fighters by 2030, India is still struggling to get the delivery of the first squadron by 4.5-generation Tejas Mk1A. Though the IAF had placed orders for a total of 180 Tejas Mk1A fighter jets long ago, HAL hopes to deliver the first 18-25 Tejas Mk1A only by March 2027.Air Marshal Kapoor (Retd) did not totally rule out the role of Tejas Mk2 in future when he said, “You can have a certain number of those 5th generation and 6th generation fighters, but given the size of the country, you won't be able to deploy them everywhere.So those gaps which continue to remain to be filled will have to be filled by this class of aircraft.” “I want Tejas Mk-2 to come, I want India’s 5th-gen AMCA to come. But they must come at a much faster speed,” he said.When asked about Russia’s 5th-gen fighter jet Su-57, the former vice-chief said when the Russian fighter is compared to western jets like American F-35, western jets have an edge over the Su-57 as they have better avionics and stealth.Air Marshal Kapoor (Retd) suggested that India should partner with an European consortium working on state-of-the-art sixth generation platforms. “There are other things that are happening — why not join FCAS (Future Combat Air System is the European programme for 6th generation jet under development by French Dassault Aviation, Airbus and Indra Sistemas) Why not GCAP (Global Combat Air Programme is a multinational initiative led by Italy, Japan, and UK to jointly develop a sixth-generation jet).“'You are probably going with a consortium which has got a good record of delivery, of development. Why go through this Gen 4, Gen 4.5 steps when you know the next best thing is already being thought of and why not just join up there?,” the IAF veteran said.
Article Summary: Air marshal nagesh kapoor (retd) has slammed the delay in the delivery of tejas (lca) fighter jet by hindustan aeronautics limited. The delivery of the indigenous lca tejas mk1a jets by hal to the iaf has faced multi-year delays, primarily caused by late supplies of f404-in20 engines by american ge.

Article Title: World in churn, and India’s foreign policy needs to adapt to it
Article Text:
Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

There is a growing sense that something is seriously amiss in India’s foreign policy. Yet, foreign policy debate is still tiptoeing around the big questions.There were three foundational assumptions that underlay Indian choices at the turn of this century. First, no great power in history had acquired such preponderance over its rivals as the US had by 2000. US primacy also meant there was no way to avoid hitching a ride with the US.Second, to make the arrangement mutually attractive, a common antagonist, China, was projected to help overcome decades of dissonance and suspicion that had divided Indians and Americans. The new discourse played on Indian ego and US greed. Washington would lift Delhi in the international pecking order, while India would generate business and arms sales for America. If everything unfolded as planned, India would become a prized Western sentinel in Asia, cementing US hegemony for the 21st century.Third, although the world economy had broadened by the early 2000s, the US was firmly at the helm in connecting the Global South to the G-7. Interdependence was a euphemism for a US-led geoeconomic order that would dominate innovation, supply chains and international trade.All three assumptions have been shattered in recent years. One, the US has not just lost its primacy, it has lost its ability to control major geopolitical events. Every roll of the dice in recent years to arrest its decline — the trade standoff with China, NATO’s confrontation with Russia, the clash against Iran — has produced a blowback that has further weakened it.Historically, the balance of power has always been ultimately revealed through major war. The present phase is no exception. The Ukraine and Iran wars have not just depleted NATO arsenals, they have exposed the doctrinal fragility of Western military power.Two, China has raced so far ahead that the rhetoric from two decades ago of an Indian ‘catch-up’ and ‘the 21st century rivalry’ appears absurd to any sober observer. The Chinese lead is not merely in aggregate economic terms but in the underlying policy institutions, human capital and technologies.And, most crucially of all, the commanding heights of the world economy are inexorably shifting towards the east. From manufacturing and high technologies to energy and natural resources, consumer demand, and financial capital, the greater Eurasian continent and its periphery have all the core requirements of sustaining a dynamic geoeconomic order without dependence on the Atlantic West. At no point in recent centuries was such a Eurasian-centred globalisation possible.But even as world events have upended the Indian foreign policy consensus, a network of gatekeepers is stubbornly impervious to change. The defenders of the failed policy erect a straw man to frighten policymakers from a thoughtful reassessment. China, they say, must remain the raison d’être of Indian policy planning even as US predatory actions seek to eviscerate the last vestiges of India’s strategic independence and authority in the subcontinent. Much has changed between 2005 — when the US pledged to help make India a “major power in the 21st century” — and 2026, when a US diplomat publicly warned that India would never be permitted to acquire the sinews of a great power. Pentagon official Elbridge Colby even had the cheek to imply that US strategic interests vis-à-vis China would not be held hostage to disputes within Asia.Must India be the only rigid actor amidst all these churnings and machinations around it? The search for a workable modus vivendi with China must acquire a bipartisan policy priority, not as an afterthought to merely prevent conflict in the Himalayas but as a means to diversify a dangerous dependence on the West. India needs to permanently discard the proxy role that it assumed during the unipolar moment and recover its regional power identity that allows for differences as well as shared responsibilities with China. The world is becoming multipolar. And such a future demands responsible Eurasian powers to safeguard world order and stability. It is in India’s vital interests to play such a role.India’s foreign policy debate can’t be stuck on an old framework, one that prides itself on managing the distance between Delhi and the great powers. There is no geopolitical room or surplus strength in any great power’s tent to underwrite India’s social, economic and security challenges. The Cold War is over. The post-Cold War era is over too. The transformation in world politics demands a new intellectual framework where sovereignty, regional interdependence, new geoeconomic networks of trade and investment, international public goods and order-building are placed at the front and centre of India’s foreign policy.To change course, Indian leaders need to look at the day after tomorrow.
Article Summary: There is a growing sense that something is seriously amiss in india’s foreign policy. Yet, foreign policy debate is still tiptoeing around the big questions. There were three foundational assumptions that underlay indian choices at the turn of this century.

Article Title: 'Deal with China confidently': Jaishankar on India strategy; lays out 3Cs, 4Ds global outlook
Article Text:
On China, Jaishankar said India should continue doing business with Beijing while developing the domestic strength needed to compete with it

Jaishankar's 3Cs view of the world

The 4Ds response

India-China ties need stability

India has raised Chinese visa concerns

NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday offered a candid assessment of a rapidly changing global landscape, warning that growing geopolitical and economic tensions are creating new challenges for countries and businesses. He also stressed that India must remain engaged with the world's major economies while strengthening its own industrial and economic capabilities.Speaking at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026, Jaishankar said the emerging global environment required countries to reduce vulnerabilities, broaden their economic options and prepare for disruptions rather than rely on assumptions of stability.He framed his assessment around three defining features of the present world order: competition, conflict and the growing use of economic and strategic leverage. To navigate these pressures, he proposed a four-part approach centred on reducing risks, diversifying partnerships and sources, addressing market distortions and maintaining a margin of safety.On China, Jaishankar said India should continue doing business with Beijing while developing the domestic strength needed to compete with it. He said greater self-reliance, industrialisation and manufacturing capacity would allow India to engage China more confidently rather than disengage from it."We have to do business with the entire world. That includes China too. But it is important we deal with them confidently."Jaishankar said India-China relations had gone through a difficult period between 2020 and 2024 because of the border situation, but both countries had an interest in maintaining stable ties. He also said India needed to make up for decades of shortcomings in building its manufacturing and industrial base."So I think a stronger, more self-reliant India, a more industrialised India, a more manufacturing India will be able to actually compete with China as it will with other major countries of the world.""It's not a very comforting answer I'm going to give," Jaishankar said while describing how he sees the world today.He said the world had become increasingly competitive, with countries and policymakers pursuing their interests to a point where competition could turn into conflict."I think what we've seen particularly in the last year or so, but I would really describe it as a growing trend. It looks increasingly competitive," he said, adding that countries and policymakers were pushing their interests "to a point where you actually have conflicts."He pointed to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the conflict in West Asia as major examples, noting that one had entered its fifth year while there was still no clear "light at the end of the tunnel" for the other.Jaishankar said competition was no longer confined to traditional geopolitical rivalry, with economic and strategic tools increasingly being "weaponised"."This is a world increasingly characterised by choke points," he said, explaining that such a choke point emerges when "a country or a set of countries have established dominance" in a particular field and are prepared to use that dominance to exert pressure.According to Jaishankar, such leverage can "inflict pain" on others, while countries exercising it may believe they are sufficiently insulated from the consequences.Jaishankar then outlined what he described as a response to these challenges."If I declare the problems in terms of Cs, maybe I move an alphabet beyond," he said, presenting derisking as his first and "biggest mantra"."Derisking will be my biggest mantra," Jaishankar said, stressing that the principle applied not only to businesses but also to politics and strategy.His second D was diversification."The more partners, the more sources that you have, clearly extending that you derisk," he said, arguing that countries and businesses should avoid excessive dependence on a small number of partners or sources.The third was dealing with distortions. Jaishankar pointed to disruptions in energy, fertiliser and shipping markets linked to conflicts and the emergence of choke points.For his final point, he urged businesses and policymakers to move beyond the traditional principle of "Trust and Verify"."Today I say 'Distrust and Diversify'," he said, arguing that planning should take into account the possibility that "things may not go right".He also warned against excessive reliance on just-in-time supply chains and the assumption that the lowest cost should always determine economic decisions."Don't let your supply chain really be just in time anymore; don't assume that your lowest cost will be the determinant," he said, stressing the importance of building a "margin of safety".Turning to China, Jaishankar said India's engagement with Beijing should ultimately help modernise the Indian economy and strengthen domestic capabilities, even as trade and other economic interactions continue."But for us, the interaction is the purpose of it is finally to modernise our economy and to develop our capabilities, but even as we do so, obviously there will be trade, there will be other economic interactions with them."He said India and China had experienced a particularly difficult phase between 2020 and 2024."I think we went through a particularly bad patch between the summer of 2020 and the autumn of 2024, and that was primarily an outcome of the situation in the border"However, he said both countries remained major economies and markets for each other, and that greater cooperation could be possible if relations remained stable and moved in a more cooperative direction.At the same time, Jaishankar said India had to address the weaknesses created by decades of inadequate industrialisation."We stand our ground as we have stood in the border. We develop our strengths, which unfortunately, as I said, from the 1960s for half a century, we did not do.""We have to make up for the shortcomings and you know the the mistakes of the past, and and that is really what we are hoping to do."Jaishankar said building a stronger manufacturing base would be central to India's ability to compete with China and other major economies.Jaishankar also acknowledged concerns among Indian businesses over difficulties obtaining Chinese business visas, saying the government had taken up the issue."So, in seeing those stories about business visa issues, which our businessmen have been facing, yes, we have seen it, and I want to say, I mean, for those of you who may have an interest or who may have been affected, we have taken it up as well."At the political and strategic level, he said both India and China had an interest in maintaining stable relations."I would also say, at a political level, at a strategic level, they, you know, it's both of us have an interest in maintaining a certain, you know, I would say stable relationship here."Jaishankar cautions against US-China 'G2' narrativeJaishankar also urged caution over the idea of a US-China "G2", saying the relationship between Washington and Beijing remained fundamentally competitive despite areas of cooperation."I think people use that term. I would advise you to treat it with some caution, because the fact is, if you look at the US-China relationship, I think at its heart it's a fundamentally competitive relationship."He said the two countries could still cooperate in some areas and remain largely indifferent to each other in others."But as is often the case, it can also be collaborative in certain matters. It can be indifferent in certain sectors."He added that the US and China would not necessarily compete on every issue, in every geography or at every point in time."So it is not that they will compete on every issue and every geography and every time flight."Jaishankar concluded that the uncertainty confronting governments and businesses represented a broader shift in the global environment."I think this is the reality of the world. It applies to national policymakers; it applies to enterprise decisions," Jaishankar said, concluding: "I think it is a realistic picture."
Article Summary: Jaishankar says india must remain engaged with the world's major economies while strengthening its own industrial and economic capabilities. He said greater self-reliance, industrialisation and manufacturing capacity would allow india to engage china more confidently.

Article Title: 'Judges are not gods, won't get every judgment right': Outgoing SC Judge Sanjay Karol in farewell speech
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Retiring Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Karol in his farewell address on Saturday, said judges "are not gods and they will not get every judgment right." He also urged other judges to look beyond the facts of a case and see the person behind every litigant.The Supreme Court bid farewell to Justice Karol on his last working day, with Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and senior members of the Bar, including Solicitor General Tushar Mehta and Supreme Court Bar Association president Pradeep Rai paying tribute to the outgoing judge.“We, as judges, are not gods. We will not get every judgment right. What was always in our hands was simple: to see the person, not just the petitioner. A petition can only tell you the facts of a case, but it cannot tell you what the person has already lost or what he is hoping to seek from the courts. And perhaps that is why I have always said that judging requires a certain level of humility,” Justice Karol said.“The Constitution does not ask us merely to apply the law correctly. It asks us to apply it justly. That is perhaps why the responsibility of judging has always seemed larger to me than simply deciding who is legally correct,” he added.Justice Karol, who was elevated to the Supreme Court on February 6, 2023, reflected on his nearly four-decade journey in the legal profession. He said the courtroom had never been merely a workplace for him, but a vehicle for something “greater and more important” than himself.“I will not pretend that this journey has been mine alone. This courtroom has not left me; it has supported me,” he said.Karol spent 40 years in courtrooms, initially as an advocate and later, for 19 years, as a judge. He said judges must learn to listen not only to arguments but also to the “eloquent silences” in courtrooms.“In the silence of the Bar, there is a way of listening,” he said, stressing that the judicial process was also about understanding what people were seeking “in the spaces between the words”.Recalling his first visit to Courtroom No. 1 of the Supreme Court in 1996, Justice Karol said the Bench appeared to him to be almost six feet above the ground.“Judging from there has taught me something about this courtroom's symbolism. From below, the height of the bench can appear to signify authority. From the comfort zone, it signifies something quite different, and that is responsibility with dignity and honesty,” he said.Justice Karol said the Supreme Court's true significance lay in the faith of ordinary citizens who approach it believing that someone would listen.“But we must also remember those who never reach those doors because justice is too distant, too expensive, too intimidating,” he said.Reflecting on constitutionalism and justice, Karol said concepts such as law, due process and constitutional legality could be understood through the idea of “dharma”, which he described not as ritual but as duty.“The duty of a judge is to respect justice and see that the person standing before the court, however small, however wretched, is seen and heard,” he said.Addressing the Bar, he said the principles of judging extended beyond courtrooms and judicial robes, with every individual responsible for judging their own choices, conduct and use of power.“There may be no courtrooms, no robes, no technical grounds, but in these small choices, each of us dispenses the measure of justice that we take,” he said.“A judge is a judge before he dons and after he takes off the robes,” he added.Referring to a point made by CJI Surya Kant a day earlier, Justice Karol said India had not only a living Constitution but also had to “live the Constitution”.“The greatness of our Constitution is tested not only in great cases. It is tested in ordinary conduct,” he said. Concluding his farewell address, Justice Karol said he was returning to “the most distinguished constitutional office," that of the ordinary citizen.Born on August 23, 1961, Karol studied in Shimla and obtained his law degree from Himachal Pradesh University. He became advocate general of Himachal Pradesh in 1998 and served until 2003, and was designated a senior advocate in 1999.He was appointed a judge of the Himachal Pradesh high court in March 2007 and became chief justice of the Tripura high court in November 2018. He was later transferred as chief justice of the Patna high court in November 2019 before being elevated to the Supreme Court in February 2023.
Article Summary: Retiring supreme court judge justice sanjay karol said judges "are not gods and they will not get every judgment right" he urged other judges to look beyond the facts of a case and see the person behind every litigant. Chief justice of india surya kant and senior members of the bar paid tribute to the outgoing judge.

Article Title: IndiGo A321neo grounded after tail impact during Gorakhpur landing
Article Text:
File photo: Airbus A321-252NX bearing registration VT-ILR

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

LUCKNOW: An IndiGo Airbus A321neo aircraft was grounded at Gorakhpur airport after suffering a tail impact during its landing approach on Wednesday afternoon.The aircraft, operating flight 6E 2381 from Delhi to Gorakhpur, was an Airbus A321-252NX bearing registration VT-ILR. The aircraft was delivered to IndiGo in August 2021.It carried out two go-arounds before making a successful landing on the third attempt at around 3.43pm as perIn a statement, IndiGo said the flight carried out a go-around during the landing approach in the interest of safety. The aircraft subsequently returned and landed safely at Gorakhpur airport. All passengers and crew members disembarked safely.“During a regular post-flight walk-around, scratches were observed around the APU inlet. The aircraft is undergoing maintenance and will resume operations after the necessary clearances,” the airline said.The aircraft has remained grounded at Gorakhpur airport since the incident.A senior official at Gorakhpur airport said the technical issue linked to the tail impact had been resolved and that the aircraft was likely to depart on Saturday. The aircraft was awaiting the required technical and regulatory clearance before being released for service.A tail impact refers to contact involving the aircraft’s tail or rear structure with a surface or object. During landing, such contact can occur if the aircraft’s nose is raised excessively during the flare, causing the rear fuselage or tail cone to come close to or touch the runway. The term is broader than “tail strike” and can also include contact with ground equipment, hangar structures, maintenance platforms or other obstacles.In this case, scratches were observed around the APU inlet, an air intake located in the aft fuselage or tail-cone area (rear section of an aircraft's main body). The inlet supplies outside air to the Auxiliary Power Unit, or APU.The APU is a small turbine engine that can provide electrical power when the main engines are shut down. It can also supply pneumatic air for engine starting and, when available, cabin air-conditioning and other aircraft systems.Sources noted that the Airbus A321's extended fuselage makes it more vulnerable to tail impacts. The Airbus A321neo has a longer fuselage, with an overall length of 44.51 metres, than most aircraft in its single-aisle category.“The APU inlet is part of the aircraft’s external fuselage structure, but it is not the fuselage itself. Any damage in this area may involve the inlet grille, surrounding fuselage skin, ducting or supporting structure. Such areas are inspected after a suspected tail impact before the aircraft is permitted to fly again,” an official source said.
Article Summary: Indigo airbus a321neo aircraft grounded at gorakhpur airport. Aircraft suffered a tail impact during its landing approach on wednesday afternoon. Scratches were observed around the apu inlet, an air intake located in the aft fuselage or tail-cone area (rear section of an aircraft's main body)

Article Title: "Erika and TPUSA are watching every single one of her shows": Candace Owens could face costly legal battle as Erika Kirk and Turning Point USA reportedly prepare for potential lawsuit

Candace Owens and Erika Kirk (Image via Getty Images)

Myron Gaines predicts Erika Kirk and TPUSA could build a case against Candace Owens

Candace Owens lawsuit prediction hinges on a higher defamation standard

A fresh wave of legal speculation is building around Candace Owens after Myron Gaines predicted that Erika Kirk and Turning Point USA could eventually pursue a costly defamation case against the conservative commentator. Gaines did not claim a lawsuit has been filed. Instead, he argued that Owens’ broadcasts may be closely documented and preserved for possible legal action after the Tyler Robinson criminal case reaches a decisive point.The claim gained attention after a social media post suggested a “Candace Owens lawsuit” could be coming. The important distinction is that Gaines presented the scenario as his own prediction, not as confirmation from Erika Kirk, TPUSA, their attorneys, or a court filing.His argument centers on timing. Gaines believes any potential legal action would be stronger after Tyler Robinson’s case is resolved and more evidence has emerged publicly. He also suggested that Owens’ past and future broadcasts could become important if a defamation dispute ever reaches court.Gaines said:“What I anticipate is this. Erika Kirk and Turning Point USA are gonna wait until Tyler Robinson is convicted.Once Tyler Robinson is convicted and more evidence comes out during a trial, I think that's when they're gonna hit Candace with the lawsuits.Best believe that fucking Erika Kirk and Turning Point USA are watching every single one of her shows, saving the videos, saving every single clip that they think is gonna be considered defamation, and they're building a case right now as we speak. I guarantee you guys. They're watching every single broadcast, anytime she insinuates that Erika Kirk was involved in a murder, or that Turning Point USA was covering it up, or anything, or when she made the comment that like, oh, you guys shouldn't donate any money to Turning Point, they're corrupt, they're going to document all of that shit, dude.They probably already have every single clip right now saved somewhere. After the trial happens, and if Tyler Robinson is found guilty, they're gonna serve her with a lawsuit. That's what I think they're angling to do right now.And I think Erika Kirk only met with Candace Owens on earlier this, late last year, I think it was. I think they met either early this year or late last year. I think she literally only met her just to check a box and say, I met with her, I tried to tell her what it was, and she's still attacking me.Because you guys got to understand, from a legal strategic perspective, that as a public figure, it is really hard for you to prove defamation. Because as a public figure, you don't have some of the same benefits that private citizens are able to enjoy when you're a private citizen. Or sorry, when you're a public figure, excuse me.”Gaines then turned to the legal challenge that would accompany such a case. In the United States, public figures generally face a demanding standard in defamation litigation. They may need to establish “actual malice,” which concerns whether a defamatory statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard for whether it was true.That does not mean Gaines’ interpretation establishes that Owens has committed defamation, nor does it prove that Erika Kirk or TPUSA intends to sue her. Those questions would depend on the specific statements involved, the evidence, applicable law and, ultimately, the courts.Gaines continued:“So the threshold for defamation when you're a public figure is significantly higher, because now you have to establish defamation with malice. So if Erika Kirk and TPUSA were to sue Candace, they would have to prove that she not only defamed Erika Kirk, but she defamed Erika Kirk with malicious intent, and she knowingly did it, contrary to knowing the truth. So that's what they're gonna have to prove.What I predict is, is they're going to build their case, wait till Tyler Robinson is convicted, wait until she says, I still think he's a patsy, and then they're gonna hit her with the fucking they're gonna hit her with the lawsuit. I like Candace, you guys know this, I get along with her. But I do think that a very expensive lawsuit is coming her way very soon from TPUSA.And then they got the money to do it, bro. An organization like that has like millions upon millions of dollars in their war chest for shit like this. And you don't think those Jewish donors will put money in to get the best lawyers to go after her? What do you think?And then not only are they going to go after Candace, because she's the, you know, the most famous, etc.She also has money. I'm sure she's making anywhere from 500,000 to a million dollars a month right now. I have no doubt in my mind she's making that kind of money right now.And then Turning Point is going to use that to say, look, look how much money she's made off of us. You got to prove damages too. They're going to say, we estimate she made, you know, 15 million dollars, because they're probably gonna have forensic accountants on their shit too.Guaranteed. And they're gonna absolutely go after her and try to collect as much money as they can. But Candace is smart.I'm sure she already has money set aside for lawsuits like this. But yeah, that's my prediction.”The final words are crucial to understanding the story: Gaines repeatedly characterized the scenario as a prediction. His comments about TPUSA’s finances, Owens’ income, potential damages and the motives or actions of donors were also his own assertions and estimates, not established facts presented in the supplied material.For now, the significance of the clip lies in the possibility Gaines raised rather than an announced legal battle. Unless Erika Kirk, Turning Point USA or their representatives confirm legal action, talk of an impending lawsuit against Candace Owens remains speculation rather than a filed case.

Gaines believes any potential legal action would be stronger after tyler robinson’s case is resolved. He also suggested that owens’ past and future broadcasts could become important if a defamation dispute ever reaches court.

Article Title: Inspiring story on motherhood: “It’s not easy. It’s been one of the most challenging things in my life” - How Erin Andrews turned years of fertility struggles into a powerful message of hope
Article Text:
Erin Andrews (Image via Imagn Images)

Erin Andrews opens up about her difficult fertility journey

Why Erin Andrews refused to hide her IVF struggles

Seinfeld

Erin Andrews and Jarret Stoll eventually welcomed their son

Erin Andrews’ motherhood story continues beyond Mack

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Erin Andrews spent years reporting from some of the biggest sporting events in America, but one of the hardest battles of her life happened far away from the cameras. Her journey toward motherhood involved years of fertility treatment, emotional setbacks and difficult choices. Instead of keeping that pain private, Andrews chose to speak openly about it, hoping her experience could make another woman feel less alone.Long before Erin Andrews became a mother, she had already spent years navigating the uncertainty of trying to build a family.In January 2023, the sportscaster spoke candidly with Us Weekly about the emotional weight of IVF and the effect it had on both her and her husband, former NHL player Jarret Stoll. She did not pretend the experience was easy.“It’s not easy. It’s been one of the most challenging things in my life, and I know in my husband’s life as well,” Andrews told Us Weekly. “I’m doing OK. We’re doing well.”Those words captured the reality of a journey that had already lasted for years.Andrews had previously revealed in a 2021 essay for Bulletin that she had been undergoing fertility treatments since she was 35.She described the process as emotionally draining and explained how isolating infertility could feel when people rarely talked openly about it.Her decision to speak publicly was not simply about telling her own story. Andrews wanted to challenge the shame that can surround fertility struggles.She explained to Us Weekly that Stoll had initially questioned why she was so open about their experience. But once Andrews began talking, she discovered just how many other people were facing similar challenges. She said she hoped conversations like those could eventually lead to support groups or foundations for people dealing with infertility.Her central message was simple: infertility should not be something people feel ashamed to discuss.The physical side of IVF became another part of Andrews’ story.With her characteristic humor, she joked about handling repeated injections better than her husband. She told Us Weekly that she could take roughly 50 needles in her stomach and keep going, while Stoll would retreat to another room and watchBehind the joke was something more serious. Andrews had discovered a strength in herself that she did not know she possessed.“You know that you’re strong and that you can deal with it and it will get better,” she said.That attitude became an important part of how she approached the uncertainty.Andrews also said humor helped her cope. Rather than pretending every day was positive, she found value in being honest with close friends. Sometimes, she explained, she could simply acknowledge that the situation was awful. On other days, she could celebrate encouraging news.That honesty made her story relatable. Fertility struggles do not follow a neat emotional script. There can be hope one day and disappointment the next.For Andrews, acknowledging both sides became part of surviving the experience.Months after Andrews spoke about her fertility struggles, her story took a life-changing turn.In July 2023, Andrews and Stoll welcomed their first child, a son named Mack, via surrogate after years of fertility challenges. The arrival marked a major moment for the couple and brought a new dimension to Andrews’ long journey toward motherhood.The birth itself was not entirely without fear.Andrews later revealed that there had been a brief emergency in the delivery room after the surrogate dilated rapidly and concerns arose about the baby’s heartbeat. The moment passed quickly, and Andrews recalled that the surrogate pushed once before Mack arrived.The memory stayed with Andrews because of what it represented. After years of treatments, setbacks and uncertainty, she was finally watching her son enter the world.She later described a photograph from that moment as a perfect picture of surrogacy. In it, Andrews was kissing the surrogate’s head while Stoll looked overwhelmed with emotion.Motherhood did not erase the complicated emotions attached to Andrews’ fertility journey.In 2024, she acknowledged that she and Stoll were considering trying for another child. Article Title: Quote of the day by Socrates: “The difficulty, my friends, is not in avoiding death, but in avoiding unrighteousness”
Article Text:
Apology

Quote of the day by Socrates: What did Socrates mean by the quote?

Why Socrates placed morality above survival

Why the quote remains relevant today

Socrates and the courage to stand by his principles

The timeless lesson

The fear of death has troubled humanity for centuries, but Socrates believed there was another danger that deserved far greater concern, compromising one's principles. In Plato's, Socrates argues that “the difficulty, my friends, is not in avoiding death, but in avoiding unrighteousness.” The remark came during his trial in Athens, when he faced the possibility of execution. Rather than treating death as the greatest evil, Socrates placed greater importance on avoiding injustice and wrongdoing. His words suggest that preserving one's moral character can matter more than protecting one's life or reputation. More than two thousand years later, the idea remains relevant in a world where people often face difficult choices between doing what is right and doing what is convenient.Socrates was drawing a distinction between physical survival and moral integrity. Avoiding death may appear to be the most obvious instinct, but he believed that fear of death should not lead a person into wrongdoing. In his view, death is something whose nature humans cannot fully know, while injustice is something a person can recognise through reason and moral judgement. His argument therefore shifts the focus away from the fear of losing one's life and towards the danger of losing one's principles.Socrates suggests that a person should be more concerned about becoming unjust than about suffering an unjust fate. The quote reflects his broader belief that a good life depends not simply on remaining alive, but on living according to virtue and conscience.Human beings naturally try to protect themselves when faced with danger. Yet Socrates questioned whether survival should always be the highest priority. There are situations in which protecting oneself may require lying, betraying someone or acting against one's principles. Socrates' philosophy suggests that such choices can carry a deeper cost than physical danger because they can damage the character of the person making them. His argument therefore presents morality as something that should not be abandoned simply because circumstances become difficult. The lesson is not that life has little value, but that survival at the expense of one's principles may come with a price that is difficult to recover from.Socrates' words can be applied to many of the moral compromises people encounter in everyday life. A person may remain silent when they know something is wrong because speaking up could threaten their career. Someone may participate in dishonest behaviour because refusing could make them unpopular or cost them an opportunity. In public life, politics, business and even personal relationships, people can sometimes face pressure to choose convenience over principle. The quote offers a different way of looking at such situations. It asks whether avoiding immediate consequences is worth compromising the values that define who we are.Socrates made this argument while defending himself against accusations in Athens. He refused to abandon his philosophical mission simply because continuing it had become dangerous. According to Plato's account in Apology, Socrates maintained that he should continue examining himself and others, even if doing so made him unpopular or placed him at risk. His eventual death became one of the most enduring examples in Western philosophy of a person refusing to surrender his principles out of fear. Whether one agrees with every aspect of his philosophy or not, his willingness to accept the consequences of his convictions explains why his words have remained influential for more than two millennia.Socrates' words ultimately offer a powerful reminder that the greatest danger is not always what can happen to us, but what we can become because of what happens to us. Fear, pressure and self-interest can tempt people to abandon principles that once seemed important. Yet Socrates believed that protecting one's moral character was more important than simply avoiding hardship or death. His question therefore remains remarkably contemporary: when circumstances force us to choose between safety and integrity, what are we willing to sacrifice? The answer, according to Socrates, should never be our sense of what is right.
Article Summary: Socrates argued that a person should be more concerned about becoming unjust than about suffering an unjust fate. The quote reflects his broader belief that a good life depends not simply on remaining alive, but on living according to virtue and conscience.
